canberra.title: ‘Raygun: Breaking Badly’ finally gives us answers around the Olympic’s most infamous performance
canberra.snippet: For two years, millions of people have been left bemused and shocked by Raygun and her iconic (?) performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics....
canberra.content:
Raygun is once again back in the spotlight with her new documentary, “Untold” Raygun: Breaking Badly. Photo: Netflix.

For two years, millions of people have been left bemused and shocked by Raygun and her iconic (?) performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In just a handful of minutes, Raygun managed to kill any future the sport of Breaking had in the Olympics with her strange kangaroo-inspired moves and over-the-top bravado.

Many who watched were embarrassed, and even more confused about how she even managed to qualify.

The ridicule reached astronomical levels worldwide, leading to rumours that her husband was on the Australian selection panel or that it was all just one big practical joke.

Up until recently, we had very few answers to how Raygun ended up on that stage, but now we’ve been given our best insight yet with Netflix’s new documentary “Untold” Raygun: Breaking Badly.

The docu series “Untold” has a history of diving into novelty athletes and their ridiculous stories.

In the past, they’ve covered the likes of Jake Paul and his boxing, the controversial Liver King and his PT program and, in the future, it will cover Mr T.

Here, they dive into Dr Rachel Gunn (Raygun) and her husband, Sam Free (Sammy Sex), and their lead-up to and fallout from the games.

With all documentaries, you want the subjects to be honest and truthful, and fortunately that’s Breaking Badly’s biggest strength.

With hindsight on her side, we see a very honest side to Raygun and her reaction to the 2024 Olympics’ most infamous moment.

Whether it be from her parents, her friends or even herself, we finally hear the dancer concede that her performance was awful, but instead of bashing her for 90 minutes, we lean into the circumstances around it.

For me, the biggest takeaway was just how underprepared Raygun was for the biggest stage in world sport. She was nervous, and because the sport was at the Games for the first time, she had little experience to draw on.

There are scenes early on where she discusses with her therapist, ‘what’s the worst that could happen?’ It’s here that we get a clear image that, while she didn’t treat the experience as a joke, she had no clue what a beast the Olympics was.

What is unique in the doco is the juxtaposition in reactions to the performance.

Raygun’s parents v her husband is the clearest example.

To this day, Sam (her husband) is still adamant that she was the best possible athlete for the games. Meanwhile, her mother and father can’t help but laugh at the entire thing.

Even Raygun herself concedes it was a poor showing.

It raises the question: was Sam the one truly deluded by her “skill”?

The most heartbreaking thing here is actually the reaction of the other B-Girls (performers) who have come to terms with the fact that the sport will never be at the Olympics again.

No one remembers who won the only gold medal for breaking – only the woman who jumped like a kangaroo and rolled on the floor.

On the surface, “Untold” Raygun: Breaking Badly may appear to be another way to cash in on the hate craze of the most meme’d moment in sporting history, but it instead gives us a very good look into how the train wreck came to pass.

For the first time, I feel like I have been given legitimate answers to the mythology of Raygun, and that’s the best thing a documentary can do.

“Untold” Raygun: Breaking Badly is now streaming on Netflix.

canberra.title: Privacy or public safety? ACT asks where the line should be drawn in mental health laws
canberra.snippet: When a person with a serious mental illness is allowed to leave a secure mental health facility, who should be told? Should a person they...
canberra.content:
Consultation on the Mental Health Act 2015 will remain open until 23 October. Photo: Region.

When a person with a serious mental illness is allowed to leave a secure mental health facility, who should be told?

Should a person they previously harmed know they are back in the community? How much should their family or carer be told about their condition? And when does the community’s right to safety outweigh a patient’s right to keep their medical information private?

These are some of the difficult questions the ACT Government is asking Canberrans as it reviews the Mental Health Act 2015.

The review covers much more than privacy.

It will examine whether existing laws provide enough protection and support for people subject to mental health and forensic mental health orders, as well as rules around emergency detention, breaches of mental health orders, sexual safety and reporting after deaths.

The review is also asking whether the ACT Chief Psychiatrist should be given the power to revoke some mental health orders when they are no longer considered necessary.

Currently, because the orders are made by ACAT (Civil and Administrative Tribunal), the Chief Psychiatrist cannot end them directly and must instead notify ACAT, which then has 72 hours to review the order.

Before doing so, the Chief Psychiatrist must consult the person’s carer and nominated person. The government notes that psychiatrists or other authorised officials already have the power to revoke mental health orders in other Australian jurisdictions and is seeking feedback on whether the ACT should adopt a similar approach.

However, one of the most complicated issues is deciding who should be given information about a mental health patient – and when.

The question has particular significance in Canberra following a number of high-profile cases involving people in the forensic mental health system.

Earlier this year, Shadow Attorney-General Chiaka Barry raised the issue in the Legislative Assembly while referring to the case of Alex Ophel.

Ophel stabbed two Australian National University students and assaulted two others in September 2023 while on day leave from the Gawanggal Mental Health Unit.

At the time, he was subject to a mental health treatment order. Six years earlier, he had attacked people in an ANU lecture theatre with a baseball bat. He was subsequently found not guilty of five counts of attempted murder because of mental impairment.

That finding is important. When someone is found not guilty because of mental impairment, they are not treated in the same way as someone convicted of a crime and sentenced to prison.

Instead, they can enter the forensic mental health system, where decisions about their treatment and when they can leave a mental health facility can involve the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT). Those hearings are generally not open to the public.

Ms Barry described the system as “counter-intuitive” and “problematic”.

“As it stands, ACAT makes a discretionary decision based on medical expert opinion,” she told the Assembly.

“This happens even when the initial court judgment has resulted in a person with a mental impairment being placed in a mental health facility.”

The government’s new consultation shows why changing that system is not straightforward.

Under ACT human rights laws, people living with mental illness have the same rights as other members of the community. That includes rights to privacy, liberty, equality and protection from medical treatment without consent.

But there are circumstances in which those rights can be limited – including when it is necessary to protect an individual or the public.

The difficult part is deciding where that line should be drawn. People who have previously been harmed by a forensic mental health patient can already receive certain information.

Under the Mental Health Act, they can register as an “affected person”. Registered people can then be notified about important developments, including relevant ACAT decisions, if the patient is released from a mental health facility, absconds or fails to return after approved leave.

The government can also provide other information if it considers it necessary for that person’s safety and wellbeing.

But the information comes with strict privacy protections. A registered affected person can be warned not to make it public, and publishing it can potentially be a criminal offence. The same privacy dilemma arises in a much more common setting – families caring for someone with mental illness.

A parent, partner or carer may be the person helping someone through a crisis, getting them to appointments or noticing when their mental health begins to deteriorate.

But that doesn’t automatically give them access to another adult’s private medical information.

The government is therefore asking whether carers need more information to properly support someone – and how that could be achieved without taking away the patient’s right to privacy.

There is another complication.

What if the person asking for information is an abusive partner or family member?

The consultation specifically asks what protections are needed when there is family violence or coercive control, so private mental health information does not end up in the hands of someone who could misuse it.

It is also looking at what happens when patients cross borders.

The ACT is considering stronger information sharing between jurisdictions so important mental health information can follow a patient when they move between health systems, while still protecting their privacy.

For Canberra, where people regularly move between ACT and NSW health services, that question has obvious practical implications.

Mental Health Minister Dr Marisa Paterson said people who had experienced the system themselves needed to be part of deciding what changed.

“No one understands the strengths and challenges of the mental health system better than the people who use it, and the families, carers and supporters who walk alongside them,” Dr Paterson said.

“Every experience and perspective matters.”

The government is particularly seeking feedback from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the LGBTQIA+ community and culturally and linguistically diverse communities.

The consultation will remain open until 23 October.

canberra.title: Cock-a-doodle-d’oh! The mysterious case of the disappearing rooster
canberra.snippet: When my husband was eight, his family dog – a Jack Russell pup named Poppy – disappeared. Growing up in a tiny hamlet in Nort...
canberra.content:
When pets leave us, do we want nothing but the truth – or to soften the blow? In my experience, the truth eventually comes home to roost. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

When my husband was eight, his family dog – a Jack Russell pup named Poppy – disappeared.

Growing up in a tiny hamlet in North Wales, this was huge news for the community, and it wasn’t long before “the whole village” was out searching the fields for Poppy.

Thank goodness, Poppy was miraculously found down a rabbit hole. With no small amount of effort, she was unearthed and returned to her loving family.

In some Final Destination-level nonsense, Poppy was run over by a truck shortly thereafter. At Christmas. While the children were performing in the local nativity play.

To limit their trauma, my poor mother-in-law smiled and clapped her way through – waiting until the children had removed their halos to tell them Poppy would be spending Christmas with Jesus.

Decades later, my husband recalls the details and tells the tale well.

As a child, the loss of a pet is a core memory-maker – no matter how the news is broken.

I still recall the horror of finding our Siamese Fighting Fish had effectively committed suicide, leaping from its – with hindsight, utterly insufficient – tank to its slow, dry death on the kitchen floor.

In our modern family life, we’ve suffered a few losses – some sudden, others naturally occurring.

We once lost three sheep to a horrific dog attack, which is a crime scene I try hard not to recall. And conversely, we recently said goodbye to our 16-year-old doggo in a manner so dignified, calm and organised, it had the air of a televised state funeral.

But goodbyes are never easy – for grown-ups or the kids.

Which is why we avoided it entirely this time when we decided to rehome our rooster.

Hear me out. Then call protective services.

Ghosting. Smoke bomb. The Irish goodbye. Whatever you call it, sometimes farewells are more trouble than they’re worth and it’s easier to simply vamoose.

This was our ethos for justifying the mysterious disappearance of Dusty the rooster, who was, in fact, an inconsiderate night owl with a formidable set of pipes and no sense of time.

Dusty came into our lives as an adorable three-day-old chick, as a gift from a well-meaning neighbour overcome by the joy on my eight-year-old daughter’s face as she beheld this little fluffball.

“You can take the chick and its mum home, if you like,” she offered.

Obviously, there was no way back from this, from my daughter’s perspective. Also, she got her impulsiveness from me. Thus, single mum and little floof joined our family.

One day, Little Dusty took a really big breath and announced himself as a prize-winning pain in our butts.

He then proceeded to wake our family – and presumably any neighbours within a 5 km radius – several times every evening.

I don’t know whether he thought it was morning, was warning of fox sightings, or was just suffering from debilitating night terrors, but this rude rooster would crow from 2 am onwards.

I love animals, but no creature is cute enough to justify this level of sleep deprivation.

With regret, Dusty was served his eviction notice via our local Facebook community noticeboard, and a kindly lady (who mustn’t require sleep) offered him new lodgings.

Now, we were faced with a decision. What to tell the children?

We umm-ed and ahh-ed over this long and hard, until eventually, three months went by.

We had let things go too far. It was now awkward.

It’s the before and after nobody wanted – but Dusty found a happy home with a deep sleeping family. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

In an astonishing demonstration of object permanence – or lack thereof – the children had not questioned the whereabouts of our midnight alarm clock.

My husband and I breathed a sigh of relief, quietly celebrating the successful smoke bomb.

Unfortunately, there is always one person at the party who draws attention to such things.

Sadly, we found a dead chicken in the enclosure this week. It’s often hard to know why a chook has given up the ghost because, as prey animals, they hide their ailments well – the stoic ol’ broads.

As such, the kids are no strangers to the occasional natural chook death, and there was no beating around the bush needed. However, the incident did uncover some ugly rooster-related questions.

Time to pay the piper.

At last, we came clean about Dusty’s eviction, his new home and the importance of a good night’s sleep.

Fortunately, our country kids took the news well, and we only left a minor dent in their trust in us. Nothing we can’t buff out, hopefully.

I suppose – decades from now – it’s a tale for them to tell.

canberra.title: From 16 to 78, the women of Diamond Phoenix are still paddling together after 20 years
canberra.snippet: When Nicola “Nicky” Hayes helped start a women’s dragon boat club in Canberra 20 years ago, there were about 25 members, mostly universit...
canberra.content:
Diamond Phoenix members training on Lake Burley Griffin. Photo: Supplied.

When Nicola “Nicky” Hayes helped start a women’s dragon boat club in Canberra 20 years ago, there were about 25 members, mostly university students and young professionals in their 20s.

Today, Diamond Phoenix Dragon Boat Club has more than 50 members. The youngest is 16 and the oldest, Kay, is 78 and has competed for both the ACT and Australia.

In between are women who arrived with no sporting experience and went on to compete at elite levels, and others who came looking for fitness but found friendships that carried them through illness, bereavement and major changes in their lives.

For Nicky, who has stayed with the club throughout its 20 years, the membership may have changed, but its original character has survived.

“I think the fun and friendship has remained the same and the focus of the club on fitness and supporting members to achieve what they want to achieve,” she said.

Diamond Phoenix began in 2006, when a small group of women decided to compete seriously without losing the supportive environment they believed a sporting club should provide. They welcomed women regardless of their sporting experience and were prepared to teach newcomers from scratch.

Nicky was one of those without a background in team sport. She went on to represent the ACT. It is a path club president Kerry Foley knows well.

“Most members come to the club with little experience or no sporting background, me included,” she said.

“They see the boats out on the lake and decide to come and try the sport. I was hooked as it is a very addictive sport.”

Kerry has since competed in an ACT crew, while several Diamond Phoenix members have gone on to represent Australia.

Kay along with another member. At 78 she is the oldest member at the club. Photo: Supplied

Diamond Phoenix members celebrate together, marking the friendships and team spirit at the heart of the club. Photo: Supplied.

Diamond Phoenix members paddle together during a training session on Lake Burley Griffin. Photo: Supplied.

Then there is 78-year-old Kay.

“Kay is our oldest member and she is truly inspirational,” Kerry said. “She is very fit and has competed in the ACT team as well as the Auroras, Australia’s National Dragon Boating Team.”

The club’s competitive ambitions remain as strong as when it began.

This year, its Senior B crew won bronze at the Australian National Dragon Boat Championships. In 2019, its Senior A crew qualified for the invitation-only Club Crew World Championships.

Next May, members will travel to Japan to compete at the 2027 World Masters Games. Dragon boating, Nicky says, can be taken at different levels, but newcomers are often surprised by just how physical it is.

“It is a sport that can be taken at your own pace but what really surprises people is how much of a whole body effort it is,” she said.

“Legs and core are equally or more important than your arms.”

But success also relies on something that distinguishes dragon boating from many other sports: nobody can do it alone. Twenty paddlers have to move together. Poor timing can slow an entire boat, while getting it right creates an experience Nicky says is difficult to describe.

“There is something wonderful about a full boat of 20 women paddling in time,” she said.

“Being on a dragon boat is both relaxing and hard work at the same time; it forces you to be mindful of what you are doing in a beautiful environment.”

That reliance on each other does not disappear when the boat returns to shore. For Nicky, the depth of those relationships became clear during a regatta when her partner suffered a massive heart attack.

As she rushed to hospital, her teammates took care of her daughter.

“Thankfully he pulled through, but I am extremely grateful to my team for the support,” she said.

Kerry experienced the same support in very different circumstances. Five years ago, she lost her sister, who had also been a member of Diamond Phoenix.

“I received great support that has led to lifelong friendships,” she said. Over the years, members have supported each other through illness and the loss of loved ones. For women who have moved to Canberra knowing few people, the club has also provided a way into a new community.

And while racing brings them together, their lives as a team extend well beyond training. Saturday paddling is followed by coffee and cake at On Lake Cafe. There are walks around Canberra, movies, dinners after Monday night training and trips together – including those built around competitions.

For first-timers, however, the introduction is deliberately gentle. New paddlers receive one-on-one coaching and are encouraged to pull their paddle out of the water and rest whenever they need to. “We want them to come back again!” Kerry said.

Some things have inevitably changed over two decades. Members have come and gone – and sometimes returned. The uniforms have changed, and this year Diamond Phoenix launched a new logo and racing shirt to mark the milestone.

On Saturday, 12 September, past and present members will gather at Grevillea Park in Barton to officially launch the club’s 20th anniversary celebrations. Among them will be Nicky, one of the women who started paddling with that small group in 2006, and women who were not even born when Diamond Phoenix began.

For Kerry, who joined nine years ago, the reason she keeps returning to the lake is considerably simpler than medals or championships.

“I am in my happy place when I am on the water in a dragon boat surrounded by my friends.”

Learn more at Diamond Phoenix Dragon Boat Club.

canberra.title: What ‘peculiarly Australian’ heritage-listed object was nestled in the Greenway grass?
canberra.snippet: A routine working bee near Tuggeranong Town Centre recently turned into a delicate walk through local history. While removing 390 metres ...
canberra.content:
6 September 2026

Start the conversation

The working bee removed parts of the old fencing in Greenway to clean up the landscape for wildlife and people alike. Photo: NPA ACT/Facebook.

A routine working bee near Tuggeranong Town Centre recently turned into a delicate walk through local history.

While removing 390 metres of old fencing at the request of ACT Parks and Conservation, National Parks Association ACT volunteers had to navigate around the heritage-listed Tuggeranong Boundary Marker Complex.

The historic site features a 790-metre drystone wall and original wire work running between Athllon Drive and the Murrumbidgee River – a century-old relic surviving in suburban Canberra.

The Tuggeranong Boundary Marker Complex contains a historic example of 19th-century Australian fencing systems. Photo: ACT Heritage Register.

NPA ACT work party convenor Martin Chalk said this meant the volunteers had to be careful not to remove the wrong fencing.

“Our advice from PCS was given to ensure that we did not remove any of the … fence from within the 50-metre curtilage of the stone wall,” he explained.

“Consequently, some 125 metres of the [designated] fence was removed from our day’s work.”

The volunteers made sure their removal work was confined to the area outside the 50-metre boundary.

According to the ACT Heritage Register, the boundary marker is associated with the Cunningham and Campbell families who were “well known landholders for almost a century”.

The dry stone wall, timber posts and wires were part of the major northern boundary of their Tuggeranong property.

“[The fence] retains historic importance as an example of fencing systems in 19th century Australia, culminating in rabbit proof fencing (a peculiarly Australian feature),” its listing noted.

“The marker is the only known drystone wall extant in the ACT remaining in its original rural setting. It provides a reminder of the early agricultural origins in the area.”

For the working bee, the 50-metre exclusion zone meant the length of fence slated for removal shrank from 390 metres to 265 metres.

“The party anticipated a difficult morning, as the fence comprised two strands of barbed wire, four strands of plain wire and mesh with African Lovegrass grown through it,” a post from NPA ACT on Facebook noted.

“However, to everyone’s relief, the ground was quite moist, and the mesh came out easily.

“After nearly four hours, the job was done, leaving behind a much-improved landscape.”

The Tuggeranong Boundary Marker is the only object of its kind listed for heritage status in the Territory.

ACT-NSW border markers located on a 20-metre-wide strip of land for about 97 km between Mt Coree and Boboyan Road/Shannons Flat Road are the only other types of markers on the register.

These date from 1913-15 and are among the earliest surviving structures built after the ACT was founded.

australia.title: Victoria police hunt for man on run after allegedly attacking brother and parents with axe
australia.snippet: Police say they believe argument took place before three people critically injured in Gippsland town of Tyers on Saturday Follow our Aust...
australia.content:
Victoria police have urged the public to remain vigilant as they search for a man who allegedly attacked his brother and parents with an axe or tomahawk.

Police issued an arrest warrant on Sunday for Peter O’Ryan, 48, whose last known location was his family’s home in the Gippsland town of Tyers.

He is alleged to have entered the Cowies Road property about 12.30pm on Saturday before attacking his brother and turning on his mother and father.

The alleged attack is believed to have occurred after an argument.

O’Ryan’s father and brother, aged 77 and 47, were airlifted to hospital with life-threatening injuries and remain in critical condition.

His mother, 74, was transported to hospital with critical injuries and remains in a stable condition.

Det Sen Sgt Rodney Findlay said police had conducted a widespread search for O’Ryan, who was alleged to have fled the scene on foot and was likely still armed.

“We are working furiously to try and bring him into custody so that we can make sure everyone’s safe and he’s held to account,” he said.

Detectives are still working to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, limited by the serious condition of O’Ryan’s alleged victims.

O’Ryan’s father and brother required immediate surgery and remained in intensive care at the Alfred Hospital. They have not regained consciousness.

His mother, meanwhile, has only been able to provide sparse details in between treatments, Findlay said.

Police released images of O’Ryan on Sunday in the hope people would recognise him and provide information about his whereabouts.

O’Ryan was of no fixed address and was known to frequent the Morwell area, police said.

They said he had been known to take refuge in abandoned properties and outhouses.

Members of the public are cautioned not to approach him and to call triple zero if they see him.

Police have also directly appealed to O’Ryan to turn himself in, saying it would be in his and the public’s best interests.

“Give yourself up, come and see us,” Findlay said.

O’Ryan was last seen wearing a black and mustard coloured jacket and carrying a black backpack.

He is Caucasian and described as being of medium build with dark grey hair.

australia.title: ‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengers
australia.snippet: Passenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issue Get our breaking news email , free ap...
australia.content:
Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when her Qantas flight ran into trouble.

The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island’s mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney, when a bang shook the cabin.

A passenger seated near the left wing soon shouted “the engine’s on fire”, Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.

Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane’s left engine in a series of rapid bursts.

“I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible,” Loch said.

“There was a lot of screaming at the time.”

As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.

“That’s what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine,” she said.

“But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming.”

Qantas flight QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.

According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.

The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.

Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.

Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff sought to comfort passengers.

“The crew were all terribly, terribly calming,” Loch said.

Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, with passengers allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.

“There were massive cheers when we landed,” Loch said.

A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.

“Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely,” they said.

“We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support.”

Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch international airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.

While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.

“I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney,” Loch said.

“It was quite traumatic.”

australia.title: Brisbane swelters under hottest September day in years as east coast faces unseasonably warm weather
australia.snippet: Queensland capital hits 34.4C as firefighters battle fast-moving bushfire in Lockyer Valley west of Ipswich Get our breaking news email ,...
australia.content:
Residents have been put on high alert as an unseasonably hot start to spring gives way to blazes and increased fire risks in the nation’s east.

Queensland fire authorities issued local fire bans for Ipswich and the Lockyer Valley on Sunday as temperatures typically seen in summer gripped the state’s south-east in early September.

Firefighters in the afternoon told residents at Plainland, west of Ipswich, to prepare to leave in response to a dangerous and fast-moving bushfire near the Warrego Highway.

The New South Wales rural fire service issued an emergency warning, which was later downgraded, for a large grass fire burning near Tabulam, in the state’s north.

Brisbane reached a high of 34.4C on Sunday, making it the hottest September day in the city since 2019.

“If we get a run of westerlies, potentially we can see some late afternoon heat if those westerlies increase and brings some hotter air out towards Brisbane from inland,” the Bureau of Meteorology’s Steve Hadley said.

Coastal areas from Gladstone to the Gold Coast came a few degrees shy of breaking the record for the state’s highest recorded temperatures for the start of spring.

The state had experienced its third-warmest winter on record with temperatures 1.8C above the long-term average.

South-east Queensland’s fire bans came a day after a similar ban was issued for the greater Sydney region, with early spring temperatures climbing to 33C on Saturday in the NSW capital.

Maximum temperatures across the city during the first days of September matched the midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since observations began.

The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) warned on Sunday of unseasonal heat in the low to mid-30s in north-eastern New South Wales and south-east Queensland.

Severe weather warnings were in place for south-eastern Australia over the weekend as damaging winds fuelled the hot conditions.

Jumping castles were picked up by strong winds in two separate incidents in NSW and Victoria on Saturday.

Two children were treated for head injuries at a scene in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, before being transported to hospital.

An infant with minor injuries was also hospitalised, while a woman was treated at the scene.

Two children in Mount Duneed, near Geelong in Victoria’s south-west, were hospitalised after the jumping castle they were using was lifted into the air.

Temperatures are expected to drop in the coming days across both NSW and Queensland.

BoM meteorologist Jonathan How said over the past 24 hours, a cold front swept across south-eastern Australia, bringing damaging winds, rain and storms.

“At the same time, parts of eastern NSW saw their warmest early spring day on record,” he said.

But a dry cool change was moving up the east coast, bringing milder temperatures from Monday. Western Australia is set to get more rain this week, while Tasmania and Victoria can expect some showers.

australia.title: Up to 6,000 tradies to get free qualifications under Labor scheme – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed. Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Duniam targets ‘frivolous’ asylum seeker claims The...
australia.content:
Tradies qualifications to be fast-tracked

Up to 6,000 tradies will get free qualifications under a $78m federal scheme designed to tackle construction skills shortages.

Workers with at least three years’ experience will have their prior learning recognised, and they will then be given “gap training” to reach their qualification, fast-tracking the process.

The skills and training minister, Andrew Giles, said the program would “back in workers who have the right skills for the job, but need that extra help to get the formal qualification they need”:

This program recognises the expertise they’ve already developed and helps them gain nationally recognised qualifications faster.

For a long time industry and skills stakeholders have called for greater recognition of existing skills and alternative pathways to formal trade qualifications – our government has listened and is taking action.

What we learned today, Sunday 6 September

That’s a wrap of our live coverage for today – thanks for being here! Today’s top stories included:

  • The Albanese government is set to unveil plans for a crackdown on the big tech companies to stop them delivering problematic or illegal content to vulnerable users. Angus Taylor has said he’s “deeply sceptical”, while Zoe Daniel says an algorithm switch isn’t enough.

  • The Coalition wants new criminal offences for burning the Australian flag, but Labor has criticised the push as having an “element of desperation”.

  • And the influence of big tobacco is under the spotlight again amid talks of cuts to excise tax.

Have a glorious evening, and we’ll see you here again tomorrow.

Queensland triple zero glitch fixed, minister says

Queensland’s health minister said a computer bug in the state’s triple zero system was just a “minor hiccup”.

The service was forced to switch to a manual backup last week after a bug emerged during a system update to a new computer aided dispatch system. Staff were required to radio crews directly and write down information manually, rather than using the system.

Health minister Tim Nicholls said that caused “some slowness in the system”, but that a patient would not have noticed any difference as a result. All low-acuity patients made to wait were monitored by the services’ clinical services hub. He said:

The alternative system kicked in. No triple zero calls were missed. There were no adverse patient events.

The care that’s being provided by the (clinical services) hub and by the [Queensland Ambulance Service] was unchanged.

He said a patch had been implemented on Friday and fixed the problem.

Flag plan not about One Nation, opposition says

The Coalition’s plan to criminalise flag burning and the defacing of historical monuments, and to enshrine 26 January in law as Australia Day, is not about trying to out-Pauline Pauline, leader Angus Taylor says:

It’s time to stand up for Australia, our heritage, our history.

Read more here from Tom McIlroy:

Queensland government announces 2,200 homes for Brisbane site

Queensland’s government has signed off on a plan for 2,200 homes in Brisbane’s north, on a site that had been earmarked for an Olympics athletes’ village.

The deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, announced five companies had won bids to build the riverfront development, at Northshore Hamilton.

The area is listed as having a high likelihood of flooding and high likelihood of storm tide flooding according to Brisbane city council’s flood mapping.

Asked if the area had a risk of flooding, Bleijie said:

That all gets taken into consideration as it does with anyone building along the river.

He said that public transport access would be taken into consideration by Economic Development Queensland, which owns the site and will be the development authority.

Taxpayers will pay $154m to prepare the site for development. It will not include any dwellings designated as affordable housing; under Labor’s plan for the site, about 5% of dwellings were mandated to be let below market rate.

The development will also include about 21,600 sq m of shops, dining and services.

Government’s plan is to ‘censor’ the internet, opposition says

Tom McIlroy has some more on the reaction to the government’s planned crackdown on big tech. Draft legislation is expected to be released this week:

Bondi car chase ends in arrest

A car chase in Bondi this morning ended with the 21-year-old driver being charged with offences including driving recklessly and hindering police.

The man had allegedly been behaving aggressively on Gould St at Bondi Beach and when police approached him he jumped in his car and took off. NSW police said the chase continued through O’Donnell St in North Bondi before the car came to a stop and the man was arrested.

He was granted conditional bail and will face Waverley local court on 22 September.

Qantas’ New Zealand flight ‘engine issue’

Customers who were on a Qantas plane that was diverted from Sydney to Christchurch yesterday will instead be flown home today.

There were reports of loud noises and flames coming out of one of the plane’s engines after it departed Queenstown. While there was a “suspected engine issue” on flight QF122, both engines were working and there was no emergency landing.

A Qantas spokesperson said the company understood it “would have been a distressing experience for passengers”:

One of our flights to Sydney experienced a suspected engine issue after take-off from Queenstown this afternoon and the aircraft diverted to Christchurch.

Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely.

South Australian native birds receive H5 bird flu jabs

Curlews and royal spoonbills are among the native bird species set to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu in South Australia.

The program at Cleland Wildlife park will see up to 100 birds across 30 different species – including threatened species – given two jabs.

The environment minister, Emily Bourke, said it was about giving them “the best chance possible”.

The lethal strain has killed thousands of wild birds, at least 100 penguins, and a dolphin. It has also infected fur seals.

Tradies qualifications to be fast-tracked

Up to 6,000 tradies will get free qualifications under a $78m federal scheme designed to tackle construction skills shortages.

Workers with at least three years’ experience will have their prior learning recognised, and they will then be given “gap training” to reach their qualification, fast-tracking the process.

The skills and training minister, Andrew Giles, said the program would “back in workers who have the right skills for the job, but need that extra help to get the formal qualification they need”:

This program recognises the expertise they’ve already developed and helps them gain nationally recognised qualifications faster.

For a long time industry and skills stakeholders have called for greater recognition of existing skills and alternative pathways to formal trade qualifications – our government has listened and is taking action.

Plan to criminalise burning of Australian flag about ‘national pride’, says Taylor

Tom McIlroy

As touched on earlier, the opposition wants new laws to make it a criminal offence to burn the Australian flag or damage war memorials.

As the Coalition fights to regain standing against Pauline Hanson and One Nation, the opposition’s legislation would create a federal criminal offence for serious public desecration of the Australian flag, where a person is reckless or where their actions would incite hatred or violence, threaten public order or cause a public disturbance.

It would also create a federal criminal offence for deliberately damaging, defacing, desecrating or destroying war memorials and other significant memorials commemorating Australia’s history.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, says the plan is about “standing up for the national pride that we should all feel for our great country.”

The assistant foreign minister, Matt Thistlethwaite, says the plan is about politics:

I think that there’s a bit of an element of desperation there, trying to chase One Nation.

It’s been tried on several occasions over many, many years. The parliament has generally always rejected it because of the notion of upholding freedom of speech for Australians and that freedom of political expression.

Nepal situation becoming more difficult with time: assistant foreign minister

Tom McIlroy

Matt Thistlethwaite, the assistant foreign minister, has told News24 there is no change in the situation of missing Australians in Nepal overnight.

He says 36 Australians still remain unaccounted for as of Sunday morning. He said:

We haven’t got any confirmed deaths yet. We’re hopeful that we’ll be able to relocate and locate as many of those as we possibly can.

Obviously, the longer this goes on, the more difficult that that becomes. But there are glimmers of hope. We managed to locate seven Australians this week.

He said it was positive that two people had been rescued from hydroelectric tunnels in the disaster area in recent days:

We sent 47 Australian personnel to the region to assist with the rescue and recovery, and we’re sending a further seven this week, so we’re doing everything we can to try and locate those Australians that are missing.

There are now 47 Australians deployed to the crisis, including seven disaster victim identification specialists and a psychologist.

More than 5,000 people are still missing and there have been 1,332 confirmed deaths.

There’s a manhunt underway in Victoria after an alleged axe attack, with three people seriously injured. Andrew Messenger has the details here:

Natasha Stott Despoja to lead inquiry into sexual violence in military

Former Democrats senator Natasha Stott Despoja, who has done a wealth of work with women and domestic violence, will lead an independent inquiry into sexual violence in the military.

The royal commission into defence and veteran suicide found there was a “systemic issue” in the Australian defence force and recommended such an inquiry.

Stott Despoja tells the ABC the issue was both systemic and underreported, possibly by more than 60%. She said the inquiry would likely report by the end of next year.

She said:

I’ll make sure that we do this in a way that is trauma informed, victim-centric, and people will have the wellbeing and the legal supports that they need.

But I do acknowledge some people have told and retold their stories, and I do not underestimate the level of trauma involved in that.

So I’m very conscious of making sure that victim-survivors are at the heart and the core of this inquiry and that they’re treated with the dignity and the respect that they deserve.

Tom McIlroy

Coalition supports compulsory superannuation: Taylor

Angus Taylor has been asked about Pauline Hanson’s calls for people facing tough financial pressures to be able to access their retirement savings.

Hanson argued earlier this month that in a cost-of-living crisis, it’s not right to force people to save for the future when they can’t make ends meet today.

Taylor has told News24 the Coalition supports the superannuation guarantee rate of 12% and notes there are already rules allowing people in financial distress to access some of their savings.

He said the Coalition had an “an open mind” on revisiting its policy to allow first homebuyers to access more of their retirement savings for a home deposit. That policy was put to voters at the 2025 election and is being considered again by the Coalition ahead of the next poll. Taylor said:

The important point I would make at this point is that we need to cap immigration based on housing supply, get more houses built, slash the red tape in the construction industry.

Tom McIlroy

Taylor unconcerned about tobacco donations to Nationals

Angus Taylor has told News24 the decision by the Nationals to take political donations from tobacco companies is a decision for the party.

The Nationals are the only major party in Australia to still accept tobacco money. The Liberals stopped accepting tobacco donations in 2013, when Tony Abbott was opposition leader.

Labor stopped taking tobacco donations in 2004.

In 2024-25, the Nationals received $225,500 from two large manufacturers. British American Tobacco donated $55,000 to the Nationals in 2022-23 for the first time in more than a decade. A year later, it sent the party $88,000.

Taylor said he wouldn’t discuss donations to the junior Coalition partner:

That’s a matter for the National party. I’m not going to get into that,” he said.

We’ve made this decision. What this is about is doing what’s right for Australia and Australians.

Excise cut plan won’t see smoking rates rise: Taylor

Tom McIlroy

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, says the Coalition’s plan for an 80% cut to tobacco excise won’t cause an increase in smoking rates, telling News 24 the new policy idea will undermine the business model of organised crime.

Asked if cheaper cigarettes will see more people take up smoking, Taylor said “the horse has already bolted on this”:

The price is already around $15 or less for most smokers, and anyone can choose to buy that. You can walk into shops all over the country and and pay $10 or $15 to buy a pack of cigarettes now.

You’ve got to recognise the reality here. This is funding organised crime.

It will disrupt the business model. It will take the profits and the customers away from organised crime in this country.

Hold the tech bros accountable, Daniel says

Here is former Goldstein MP Zoe Daniel’s take on social media: she says a “digital duty of care must hold the tech bros accountable for the safety of the spaces that they have created”:

[Legislation] could also include misinformation and disinformation. This would risk the usual culture war debate about free speech, while we blithely accept the changes to our culture and society that are being freely imposed by Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and others.

What we should be worried about is the sovereignty of the information landscape and the fact that we’re being controlled by the systems – not the other way around.

Hefty fines for social media companies under government plan

The onus will be on social media companies to identify and mitigate risks on their platforms under the government’s proposed legislation, Insiders host David Speers says, and that legislation will be unveiled this week.

He says it will cover illegal content including illegal pornography being made available to adults, and for kids there would be “around half a dozen additional areas of psychosocial harm and that includes content around body image and bullying”.

He says:

The companies would face hefty fines of more than $100m if they fail to restrict this content and as for algorithms – regular pop-up messages would be required, asking if users want to stick with the algorithm or only see people they’re following and see what they’re posting. The user would have the choice.

Researchers and the eSafety commissioner would also be empowered to police the social media platforms by using what are called ‘sock puppets’ posing as children to monitor what is being fed to kids online.

You can read the background to this legislation here:

Opposition will have a ‘humdinger’ immigration policy, Duniam says

Insiders host David Speers asks Duniam about the opposition’s proposal to criminalise flag burning. Duniam says it’s a “good idea” and talks about American patriotism. He says the move would help with the immigration debate:

One of the problems we have is ‘who are we?’, ‘who are we inviting you to be part of?’

If we stood up for who we are and were proud as a nation, we could get onboard and deal with issues that flow out of immigration.

Duniam is leaving parliament at the end of the year and says his legacy will include a “humdinger” immigration policy and his work on artificial intelligence. Asked for his advice to his party, he says they have to keep an eye on their foundational values and give people a good reason to vote for them by coming up with policies that capture the imagination:

Don’t act like a government in exile. We are the opposition and we have a hell of a fight to get back to government.

australia.title: Labor plans crackdown on social media algorithms as Taylor says he’s ‘deeply sceptical’
australia.snippet: Anika Wells expected to release legislation creating a digital duty of care in parliament this week, but Coalition argues it is ‘attempt ...
australia.content:
Labor’s plan to crack down on social media algorithms faces significant opposition in federal parliament, with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, warning against efforts by the government to “censor” free speech online.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, is expected to release draft legislation creating a digital duty of care for social media users in Australia as parliament returns this week.

Among new rules being considered are functions requiring popular social media platforms to allow users to turn off algorithms controlling the content in their feeds, and to better identify problematic or illegal content to protect vulnerable users including children.

Opt-out options for algorithms would give users the choice to make their social media feeds only feature content from friends and groups they choose to follow.

Labor wants to better protect social media users from being fed content that reinforces dangerous stereotypes and behaviours, including in areas around body image, women’s safety and child protection.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Fines of more than $100m would be created for breaches, with new powers given to the eSafety commissioner and researchers to investigate compliance by big platforms.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to spruik the plan at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.

Taylor told News24 on Sunday the government should focus on fixing problems with its under 16s social media ban before taking on new rules like the digital duty of care.

“I think everyone’s very disappointed at the way the government has implemented the initiatives to stop young Australians from getting access to social media,” he said.

“It’s something like a 4.4% reduction we’ve seen, which is just immaterial in the scheme of things. What we want to see is parents having more control over what the kids get to see on social media.

“We’ll wait and see this legislation. I’m deeply sceptical. I fear that this is just going to be an attempt by the government to censor social media.”

He warned against the communications minister having “enormous” discretion in any new powers.

“I fear, given Labor and the minister’s past biases, that this will just be an attempt to censor the internet, and that’s not what we should be doing.”

The shadow home affairs minister, the outgoing Liberal senator Jonno Duniam, likened the government’s plans to dumped anti-misinformation legislation introduced during Labor’s first term in government.

“Empowering individuals to make a choice about what they consume is absolutely where we should be at,” he said. “Empowering parents to do the same for those that are in their custody, their kids, should absolutely absolutely do something.”

Duniam told ABC TV the Coalition would only support the plan if “it doesn’t necessarily impede on people’s rights and freedoms.”

“I think that we probably already have in terms of our broadcast, free to air, film, and cinema, and other forms of media classification program, a good sort of baseline to go from.”

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has already criticised the government’s plan, warning Labor should not have control over what Australians see online.

“Australia should be moving away from government censorship, not building the Orwellian machinery for it,” Hanson posted on social media last week.

Given the opposition from the Coalition and One Nation, any new legislation would require support from the Greens to pass the Senate.

The Greens have called for opt-in rules, like those supported by campaigner Chanel Contos. That model would require social media users to give explicit consent to platforms before being subject to algorithm-based content in their feed.

world.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
world.snippet: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known...
world.content:
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.

The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.

The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.

The verdict is subject to appeal.

Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

world.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
world.snippet: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has ...
world.content:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

world.title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border Europe live – latest update...
world.content:
Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.

The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.

“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.

Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.

But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.

Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.

Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.

In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.

Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.

Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.

In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”

It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.

There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.

However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.

“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

world.title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation
world.snippet: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa The day dawned b...
world.content:
The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.

Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.

Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.

The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.

As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.

Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.

The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.

In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.

Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.

In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”

In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.

The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.

The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.

Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.

“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”

The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.

Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”

Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.

Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.

Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.

“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

world.title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
world.snippet: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have appr...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.

Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”

Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.

“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.
